idiom_name: struct field void (*update)(Entity *, double dt) walked by a for loop
implementation_notes: C has no methods and no virtual dispatch, so the pattern's hook is a function pointer stored with the data: cppreference records that 'pointers to functions are objects and thus can be stored in arrays, copied, assigned, passed to other functions as arguments' and that a function pointer 'can be used on the left-hand side of the function call operator'. What replaces the classic structure: nothing is provided - the abstract update() becomes a per-object function-pointer field (or a per-kind table of function pointers shared by all instances of a kind), the entity manager becomes the array itself, and the driver is the loop that calls each element's hook with dt. The function-pointer form is still the right choice when behaviour must be swapped per instance or per pool at runtime; for a closed set of kinds, a kind tag plus a switch is faster (no per-object pointer, no indirect call, better locality) and is what data-oriented C code does instead.
pitfalls: dt must be a parameter, not a global or a clock read: a step that fetches its own time cannot be stepped at a fixed rate and cannot be tested without a clock.
A NULL update pointer is C's spelling of a dormant object; check it (or keep dormant entities out of the array) or the driver crashes mid-frame.

Removing an entity shifts every later element down, so the next entity is skipped, and adding during the walk lets the new entity act in the frame that created it; mark dead and compact after the walk, or iterate backwards.

One function pointer per object costs storage plus an indirect call the optimiser cannot inline; with a closed kind set, a tag plus switch (or a per-kind handler table) restores inlining and locality.
